posts.alt: Replacing a Vendor-Run Telecom Ledger
posts.caption: 90,000 SMS checks per second, answered in 10 ms. In 16 weeks. A licensed Indian telecom operator wants to own its TRAI DLT platform instead of renting it from a vendor. The plan keeps the blockchain off the live path, so every SMS verdict is a local lookup. It also ships in 16 weeks with a shadow run before cut-over.
posts.body:
90,000 SMS checks a second, answered in 10 ms
Scoping a DLT platform that a telecom operator finally owns.

The problem: a vendor holds the keys
An incumbent vendor built the panel and scrubbing, runs the Fabric layer and holds the Client's ledger keys. Its IP ownership is unconfirmed since 2022.

Traffic to scrub
5-6 billion
SMS a month, plus 30 crore voice calls. Today one application node does it all, and the SMSC waits up to 120 s.

Key idea: keep the ledger off the live path
Registry changes go through Fabric chaincode. Committed blocks stream via Kafka into memory in every scrubbing node, so each verdict is a local lookup.

Targets at cut-over
90,000 TPS SMS per site
p99 of 10 ms SMS, 20 ms voice
99.99% availability
Fabric 2.5 LTS, five peers, three sites
Traffic moves in 30 s if a site fails

Going live safely
Weeks 12-14: a passive network tap copies live traffic for a shadow run. Weeks 14-16: four waves of cut-over. The third-party fallback stays throughout.

Takeaway
Own the core, keep the ledger off the hot path, and prove it with a shadow run before any traffic moves.

posts.alt: Two Ways to Get Google Meet Transcripts
posts.caption: One Meet call, two transcripts. Which one wins? Meet Transcripts is a Next.js app that pulls Google Meet transcripts two ways: a self-hosted bot that reads live captions, and Google's own Meet REST API. Both are normalized into one shape and shown in one view, so you can run both on the same meeting and compare. Every call stays on the server, so no key reaches the browser.
posts.body:
One Meet call, two transcripts. Which one wins?
A Next.js app that gets Google Meet transcripts via a bot and via Google's own API.

Way 1: send a bot
Self-hosted Attendee joins the call as a guest and reads Meet's live captions. Works on any Meet link, any account.
Live, while the call runs
Needs Docker
Someone must admit the bot from the lobby

Way 2: ask Google
The Meet REST API returns the transcript Meet made itself. Invisible in the call, but more restricted.
Only meetings you organized
Transcription must be turned on
Available after the call, kept 30 days
Needs a Workspace plan with Meet transcripts

How the bot works
POST /bots with the Meet link and caption settings
Recording format is none, so no S3 bucket
Bot waits in the lobby until admitted
Page re-reads the transcript every 3 seconds until ended

Setup time warning
10 to 20 min
First Attendee build needs about 6 GB of Docker disk. Its image is linux/amd64, so Apple Silicon runs it under emulation.

The trick: one shared shape
Both sources become the same TranscriptLine type and render in the same view. Run both on one meeting and compare them side by side.

Takeaway
Bot for any meeting, live. API for your own meetings, invisible. Same view for both. All calls stay server-side.

posts.alt: SPACE: Sandboxes for Agent Code
posts.caption: Every agent needs a safe place to run code. This is one. SPACE (Sandboxed Platform for Agentic Code Execution) runs code in isolated Firecracker microVMs behind a simple HTTP API. Your app decides what to run, and SPACE handles the sandbox, its processes, and the output stream. It is written in Rust, but you only need HTTP to use it.
posts.body:
Every agent needs a safe place to run code
SPACE: a sandbox platform built on Firecracker microVMs.

What it is
SPACE stands for Sandboxed Platform for Agentic Code Execution. Apps use an HTTP API to create Linux environments, run commands, and collect output.

How it works
A template is the starting environment. A sandbox is an instance with its own VM and writable filesystem.
Create sandbox from a template
Wait for readiness
Create a command session and attach
Keep, pause, or suspend, then wake
Delete the sandbox

Two separate channels
Lifecycle changes are async: the API returns an operation ID you poll. Command output uses a separate data-plane connection with a session-scoped token.

Built for real operations
The repo goes well beyond the core API.
Warm pools skip cold boots
Base snapshots restore sandboxes
Typed events rebuild sandbox timelines
Feature flags work with no backend
E2B compatibility wrapper

Benchmarked suspend and restore
4 profiles
Build, alloc-free, file-heavy, and idle workloads. Every cycle checks SHA-256 checksums so a memory mismatch counts as a correctness failure.

The takeaway
Your app decides what to run. SPACE manages the sandbox, the processes, and the output stream. No Rust embedding needed.

posts.alt: quirq iOS: one page, one blocker
posts.caption: An iPhone 17 Pro the newest Xcode could not talk to quirq iOS is a one page SwiftUI app with a build stamp, made to prove a phone-to-Claude build loop. The loop hit a real wall: Xcode 16.4 cannot support the iPhone 17 Pro's A19 Pro chip. Small app, useful lesson about toolchain versions.
posts.body:
The phone Xcode could not see
quirq iOS: a one page app built to test a device loop.

What the app is
One screen: the quirq mark, the name, and the line "watch the work, not the meter". Colors come from the quirq site.

The build stamp
A faint stamp shows version, build number and the time the binary was made, like v0.1 (3) · Oct 20 22:41. It matches each install to its change.

The device loop
Setup once, then repeat each round.
Add Apple Account in Xcode
Trust the iPhone, enable Developer Mode
Claude builds a signed copy and bumps the build number
Claude installs it over cable or network
Check the stamp, then request changes

The mark is pure code
The q is drawn in SwiftUI: a ring, a stem and a rounded foot, with a hole subtracted from the bowl. No image needed.

The blocker
0x8140 vs 0x8150
Xcode 16.4 supports chips up to the A18 Pro (0x8140). The iPhone 17 Pro's A19 Pro is 0x8150, so it cannot mount, register or build.

Takeaway
The fix is a newer Xcode: macOS 27.0.1 with Xcode 27, or Sequoia 15.8.1 with Xcode 26.3. Check device support before you plan a device loop.

posts.alt: One repo, one branch per experiment
posts.caption: 27 experiments live in one repo. Each one is its own branch. A repo that turns every experiment folder into its own git branch. Main is the index, finished work gets squashed into an archive branch, and publishing never rewrites history. It keeps a pile of side projects tidy without 27 separate repos.
posts.body:
27 experiments, 1 repo, 0 clutter
Every folder becomes its own branch.

Folder in, branch out
Run ./publish and each experiment folder turns into a branch with the same name. Clone a branch and you get the folder back.

Branch rules
Names can be paths, like agentic-ai/autoquirq
Group folders never become branches
Branches are orphans with no shared history
Commits only append, never rewrite

Smart about what it ships
The folder's .gitignore applies, and .publishignore always wins. Files over 100 MB are skipped and named in the commit message.

Clones become pointers
A clean clone of someone else's repo publishes a README with the upstream URL and exact commit instead of a copy.

Finished work gets archived
1 commit
./archive squashes a branch into one commit on the archive branch, then deletes the branch. archive~1, archive~2 step back through time.

Takeaway
Treat experiments as branches, not repos. You get history, an index, and a cleanup path with three small commands.

posts.alt: Space Walk: replay agent sessions as light on a map
posts.caption: What if you could watch an AI agent think through your codebase? Space Walk draws your repo as a night map and replays a coding-agent session as light moving through it. Where the agent searched, read, and edited, the map glows. It also has an optional judge that scores the session, with verdicts computed by code, not by the model. Fully local for viewing.
posts.body:
Watch an AI agent think through your codebase
Space Walk replays coding-agent sessions on a 3D night map of your repo.

The problem
A session log shows what an agent did, not how it understood the task. Raw JSONL won't tell you where it explored or whether its footprint matched your scope.

The idea: light on a dark map
Search, read, and edit moments make files glow. Everything untouched stays dark, so the agent's understanding becomes a shape you see at a glance.

Touch states
Each file keeps its deepest touch.
Seen: olive
Read: steel blue
Edited: lime
Unvisited: dark
Deleted files linger as wireframe ghosts

One local Go binary
3 agents
Reads Claude Code, Codex, and pi session logs. Viewing sends nothing anywhere.

Verdicts are never the model's
An optional judge scores four fixed dimensions plus criteria drafted from your own request. Go rolls up verdicts mechanically from finding severities, and every finding must cite real events.

Takeaway
An unverifiable criterion is a blind spot, not a failure. Space Walk shows what the agent did, and is honest about what the log can't show.

posts.alt: One UI, Two Coding Engines
posts.caption: One desktop app, two AI engines, zero UI changes Workbench is a Codex-style desktop app that runs both Codex and Claude Code behind a single interface. The trick: a small server makes Claude speak the Codex app-server protocol, so the app needs only one client, one transcript reducer and one set of components.
posts.body:
One desktop app, two AI engines, zero UI changes
Workbench puts Codex and Claude Code behind the same interface.

The idea
Workbench is a Codex-style Electron app. Pick an engine per thread: Codex or Claude. Each thread stays pinned to the engine it started on.

The trick: one protocol
Both engines speak the Codex app-server JSON-RPC (v2), newline-delimited over stdio. claude-app-server implements the subset Workbench uses.

How Claude plugs in
thread/start: new UUID as sessionId
thread/resume: resume with threadId
turn/start: one query() per turn
turn/interrupt: AbortController.abort()
Approvals: canUseTool callback

Access presets map to permission modes
Read only: plan
Ask (untrusted): default
On request: acceptEdits
Never + full access: bypassPermissions

Engine-agnostic by design
1 reducer
One client, one transcript reducer and one set of components. Main persists transcripts, the renderer draws them, both use the same code.

Takeaway
Pick one wire protocol and adapt the engines to it. Adding a new engine then means writing a server, not rebuilding the UI.

posts.alt: REA: Reverse Engineer Anything
posts.caption: See a feature you love in an app? Have your agent reverse engineer it. REA is one MCP server that lets your AI agent inspect apps without their source code. It explains how a feature works, shows the evidence, and builds a version for your project. Analysis runs locally, and every conclusion comes with its limits.
posts.body:
See a feature you love? Reverse engineer it.
REA: one MCP for binaries, apps, and runtime behavior.

The idea
Ask your agent to investigate an app with REA. It inspects the app without source code, explains the feature, shows evidence, and builds a version for your project.

What it can inspect
Same tools work from your terminal too.
Native binaries
JavaScript and Electron apps
NET assemblies
Websites

How it works
Your agent calls REA through MCP to inspect the target and trace relevant code. REA returns findings with evidence. The agent uses them to explain, implement, and test.

Evidence, not guesses
Results include the evidence and limitations behind each conclusion. Analysis runs locally on your machine.

Get started in minutes
Works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Grok Build and more.
Run: npx rea-agents setup
Pick your agents and approve changes
Restart your agent
Ask about a feature in any app

Takeaway
Understand how any feature works, down to the binary level, then build your own version.

posts.alt: Claude Messages: iMessage for Claude Code
posts.caption: What if every Claude Code session on your machine were a text thread? Claude Messages is a tiny local app that shows every running Claude Code session as an iMessage-style thread. Pick one, read its conversation, and message it, or start a new session with the compose button. It has zero dependencies and just needs Node 18 and the claude CLI.
posts.body:
What if every Claude Code session were a text thread?
Claude Messages: an iMessage-style window onto every session on your machine.

One sidebar, every session
Live sessions are listed on the left. Each thread shows that session's conversation, and you can message any of them. Compose starts a new one.

Where the data comes from
Session list: ~/.claude/sessions/<pid>.json
Thread: the session's .jsonl transcript
Read from the last 1.5 MB, then followed
Typing dots: the record's busy status

How messages get sent
Sessions started here: a user line on stdin (stream-json)
Any other session: one frame on its inbox socket
Same socket sessions use for SendMessage
Tool approvals appear as Allow and Deny bubbles

Locked down by default
Listens on 127.0.0.1 only. Rejects other Host headers and foreign Origins. Every API call needs a token that changes per launch. Key files are never read.

Dependencies to install
0
Run node server.mjs, open 127.0.0.1:4417. Needs Node 18+ and claude on your PATH.

The honest catch
Messages to sessions you did not start arrive as from another Claude session, so they count as a teammate's request, not your approval. It also relies on undocumented internals, checked on 2.1.260 and 2.1.293.

posts.alt: Innernet: your folders as a web
posts.caption: What if your folders were their own internet? Innernet crawls the folders on your machine into a search engine and an encyclopedia called Innerpedia. Search by name, language or README text, then read an article on what a project does and how it changed. Everything stays local unless you connect your own database.
posts.body:
What if your folders were their own internet?
Innernet: a personal internet, made from your folders.

One real crawl
5,484
folders indexed from one root, ~/Programming. 958 became articles, 172 are Git repos. The rest are stubs.

How it works
Crawler reads READMEs, manifests, Git metadata
Writes one local JSON index
Search finds a project (MiniSearch, on the server)
Innerpedia tells its story as an article

Projects and agents
Any folder starting with a dot (.claude, .codex, .cursor) is an agent's. Its article shows instructions and memory, and session counts. Session contents are never read.

Familiar by design
Google-style results, blue links, a knowledge panel. Wikipedia-style pages with infobox, contents, categories and See also. Mood: a private library in morning light.

Private by default
Server binds to 127.0.0.1 only
Credential folders like .ssh and .aws are never entered
Generated folders are skipped
Data leaves only if you connect your own remote database

Takeaway
Your folders already hold a web of what you built. Innernet just lets you search it and read it.

posts.alt: Brand DNA: A World Behind Every Brand
posts.caption: Type any website. Get a whole brand world back. Brand DNA is a Next.js prototype that turns a website into an explorable brand world: a social-style feed, a media library, and a brand profile. The redesign leans on a dark, peach-accented look, with AI-generated cover art made to leave room for UI text. It shows how brand data can feel like a place to browse, not a spec sheet.
posts.body:
Type any website. Get a whole brand world back.
Brand DNA: explore the colors, stories, voice and visuals of a brand.

What it is
A Next.js 16 and React 19 app where you enter a site like stripe.com and it opens that brand as a browsable world.
Search bar takes any domain
Demo starts on vercel.com
Sidebar lists example worlds

Four ways to explore
The sidebar splits a brand into four views.
The feed
Media library
Brand profile
Saved

Four story chapters
Brand data is told as short stories, each with its own headline.
01 The big picture
02 The visual language
03 The way it sounds
04 What it stands for

A media library that feels like streaming
Visual references sit on scrollable shelves sorted into Imagery, Product and Inspiration, with a featured hero: "Every frame. A feeling."

The cover art was prompted for the UI
A smoky glass and chrome ribbon with peach edges, placed on the right so the left third stays dark and clean for readable text.

Takeaway
Behind every brand, there's a whole world. Present brand data as a place to explore, not a spec sheet.

posts.alt: HEPHAESTUS: 5,000 Years of Computing
posts.caption: I made a 110s film of 5,000 years of computing. Every frame is code. HEPHAESTUS is a vertical film that runs from the abacus to reasoning machines in 17 engraved plates. It is built from data, SVG diagrams and one paused GSAP timeline, so every frame is deterministic. The scenes get shorter as history speeds up, so the film itself accelerates.
posts.body:
5,000 years of the thinking machine, in 110 seconds
HEPHAESTUS: a 9:16 film from pebbles to reasoning machines.

One accelerating project
The message: computing is a single story, from counting stones to thinking machines. Seven Latin chapters tell it, from CALCULUS to MENS, ending on one word: COGITO.

17 engraved plates
17
From the Abacus (c. 2500 BC) and Antikythera, through Note G and ENIAC, to the Transformer and machines that reason.

Two ages, two looks
The look changes with the technology.
I to III: aged paper, ink and red accent
IV to VII: gold on black
Chromatic aberration on every cut
Film grain and flicker throughout
A log-scale year ruler along the bottom

The film speeds up
5.5s to 4.0s
Scene length shrinks chapter by chapter, so the pacing itself accelerates. A running ops/second index climbs the whole way.

How it is built
Data and timing live in film.mjs. A build script writes index.html from layered SVG diagrams. One paused GSAP timeline drives it, so it is seek-safe and deterministic.

Take away
"Golden handmaids, forged by Hephaestus: in them is understanding." Homer opens the film. The machine learns to think.

posts.alt: Jev: a model that only returns probabilities
posts.caption: An AI model that never writes a word. It only returns probabilities. Jev is TypeSafe's first "System One" model. You send text plus typed questions, and it returns calibrated probabilities instead of prose. Your code owns the workflow and Jev makes the quick judgment calls, like a smart if-statement. This hello world repo shows it routing support messages, fanning out 25 questions in one call, and more.
posts.body:
An AI that never writes a word
Meet Jev: text in, probabilities out.

Questions in, typed answers out
Send a state (string or JSON) plus typed questions. Jev answers all of them in one pass.
Noul: is this true? (0 to 1)
Choice: pick from up to 255 options
Score: place on a 2 to 10 level scale

A smart if-statement
Your code owns the workflow. Jev makes the judgment calls. Plain ifs branch on confidence: act, confirm, or escalate.
Order lookup: low bar
Issuing a refund: needs confidence above 0.9
Unsure: ask a clarifying question

25 questions, about the time of 1
25 ≈ 1
Every question runs in parallel on one read of the state. TypeSafe quotes 70 to 500 ms per call.

Cheap, and output is free
$0.042
Per million input tokens. Output tokens cost nothing. Probabilities are calibrated with RLCD, so 0.8 should be right about 80% of the time.

Where it is weak
By TypeSafe's own account. Keep these in code or use an LLM.
Math and counting
Comparing dates
Multi-step reasoning
Adversarial text
Generating anything

Fast judgment, cheap enough to use everywhere
System One is Kahneman's fast thinking. Jev is named for Jevons: make it cheap and usage explodes.

posts.alt: Claude Drives the iOS Simulator
posts.caption: One SwiftUI screen where every card is something Claude can do Hello Sim is a one-screen SwiftUI app built to show what Claude can do inside the iOS Simulator. Each card is one capability, tagged with the simulator action that drives it. The same project also holds XO Space, a native sample dashboard with a plan to reach the App Store.
posts.body:
One screen. Every card is something Claude can do.
Hello Sim: a SwiftUI app that tests an AI driving the iOS Simulator.

Cards map to actions
Each card has a tag naming the simulator action behind it.
Tap: tap
Type: text
Swipe: swipe
Drag: touch_path (one finger)
Pinch: touch2_path (two fingers)

Beyond touch
Claude can build and launch the app, read screenshots, open deep links and press Home, Lock, Side, Siri or Apple Pay buttons.

Edge swipes are system gestures
A swipe starting within 4 points of an edge acts as the system gesture: left goes back, top opens Notification Center, bottom goes Home.

Command line extras
For what the panel misses, Claude runs xcrun simctl.
Dark mode
Fake GPS location
Push notifications
Screen recordings
Clean 9:41 status bar

Honest limits
Simulators only. No camera, no Face ID. The inspect action is rejected in this build, so Claude finds tap spots from screenshots.

Takeaway
A purpose-built test app turns vague AI capability claims into cards you can tap, drag and check.

posts.alt: Three Web Components, Zero Build Step
posts.caption: Three UI widgets. One file each. No npm, no build, no dependencies. shipnotes-demo is a runnable tour of three drop-in Web Components from Ship Notes: a pull-cord lamp, a particle status orb and a 3D card stack. Each is a single JS file with Shadow DOM. The demo also documents the gotchas, like React 19 crashing on the orb.
posts.body:
Three UI widgets. One file each. No build.
A tour of the Ship Notes Web Components: copy a file, add a script tag, use the tag.

Meet the trio
MIT licensed, vendored unmodified.
pull-lamp: SVG lamp, pull the cord to switch theme
signal-orb: WebGL particle status light for AI apps
project-stack: three 3D cards with tabs

Particles in the orb
12,000
6k on touch devices, with a Canvas 2D fallback if WebGL is missing. Four states: listening, thinking, searching, done.

Attributes in, events out
The page owns state. Changes made from code never echo back as events, so the lamp and page can't loop. Only the lamp emits anything (themechange).

Gotchas found while wiring
Fix for React: set attributes via a ref.
React 19 crashes on <signal-orb state=...>: getters, no setters
React event props are case-sensitive: onthemechange
Stack needs exactly 3 items or shows its sample
Orb's particle budget only steps down, never recovers

Built for safety and video
Text goes in via textContent, accents must be #rrggbb, links must be http(s). A recording attribute renders clean frames for build videos.

Takeaway
Custom elements with Shadow DOM are the lowest-friction way to share UI. Just mind the framework edges, like React 19 property setting.

posts.alt: Laya: Decisions in One Forward Pass
posts.caption: A decision engine that answers in 33 ms and never generates a word Laya is a non-autoregressive decision engine. It answers typed questions over text, emails, tickets or JSON in a single forward pass, so there is nothing to parse and nothing to hallucinate. The benchmarks are candid too: the English model reads Khmer at 0.000 accuracy while reporting 0.952 confidence, which is why routing happens before inference.
posts.body:
33 ms decisions, zero text generated
Meet Laya: a System 1 decision engine for 100+ languages.

What it is
An encoder plus a decision head answers typed questions over any state in one forward pass. No generation, so nothing to parse or hallucinate.
choice: pick a label
score: ordinal level
noul: calibrated P(true)

Speed on a T4
33 ms
One question takes 32.8 ms. Batched, it drops to 7.2 ms per question.

Three checkpoints, one router
A Router picks the checkpoint per request.
laya: ModernBERT-large, 421M, English
laya-multilingual: mmBERT-base, 322M, 100+ langs
laya-typed-decisions: 421M, 1024 context

Routing is the insight
23 to 45
Languages clearing 3x random on MASSIVE intent (of 51) once routing sends text to the multilingual model.

Confidence can lie
On Khmer, the English checkpoint scored 0.000 accuracy at 0.952 mean confidence. Confidence gating cannot catch it, so routing must come first.

Honest about limits
Base checkpoints are near chance zero-shot on typed-decisions: 0.362 against a 0.318 random baseline. The published 0.766 comes from fine-tuning. Treat Laya as a fast base to specialise.

posts.alt: Code Runs in Throwaway MicroVMs
posts.caption: Give an AI a whole desktop. Then throw it away. Three small Vercel Sandbox experiments. One lets Claude drive a real Chrome desktop. Two let you write code in a browser and run it in an isolated, ephemeral MicroVM. The idea: untrusted or AI-written code gets its own disposable machine, so nothing it does touches yours.
posts.body:
Give an AI a whole desktop. Then throw it away.
Three experiments with Vercel Sandbox MicroVMs.

Claude drives a real desktop
The AI SDK computer use demo pairs Claude Sonnet 4.5 with a remote desktop in a Vercel Sandbox. Claude uses a computer tool (screenshot, click, type, scroll) and a bash tool.

What is inside the desktop
Xvnc: virtual X11 display
openbox: lightweight window manager
noVNC + websockify: streams to your browser
Google Chrome: auto-launched
xdotool + ImageMagick: mouse, keys, screenshots

Boots from a snapshot
~10 min
Building the snapshot takes about 10 minutes, once. After that, sandboxes boot in seconds because the desktop is pre-installed.

Deploy code in one click
The Sandbox Deployer lets you write Node.js or Python in a browser editor and run it in an isolated Firecracker MicroVM. Scripts return stdout and stderr. Add a port and you get a live HTTPS URL.

Python needs a bridge
The @vercel/sandbox SDK is TypeScript-only. So the FastAPI backend calls a small Node.js script by subprocess, with a 120 second timeout, and reads JSON back.

Disposable by design
Sandboxes are ephemeral and auto-terminate after 5 minutes. Let agents and untrusted code run wild, then toss the machine.

posts.alt: Makepad: Rust UI plus AI, one engine
posts.caption: A Rust UI engine that also runs your AI models and a 3D physics engine Makepad is an AI-accelerated app and game environment for Rust. One repo holds a cross-platform UI runtime, native AI backends, a pure-Rust 3D physics port, and a standalone asset server. The physics engine beat Rapier on eight of nine benchmark scenes.
posts.body:
A Rust UI engine that also runs AI models and 3D physics
Inside the Makepad repo

What Makepad is
An AI-accelerated app and game environment for Rust, with a live-editable design language and a fast iteration loop.
Native and web targets
Scriptable UI DSL
GPU 2D and 3D rendering
Runs on iOS, Android, wasm, Quest

Faster than Rapier
8 of 9
Its pure-Rust port of Box3D beat Rapier on eight of nine benchmark scenes, +33% geomean, using zero external crates.

Deterministic and close to C
Bit-exact results across architectures, within about 7% of the hand-tuned C original. Rapier's SIMD and determinism modes cannot be combined.
Washer is the one scene Rapier wins
Mesh scenes: up to +136% over Rapier

AI runs natively, no Python
The pixal3d backend turns an image into a textured 3D mesh in Rust and CUDA. Production inference does not start ComfyUI or Python.
Image to PBR GLB export
Matting, shape diffusion, decoders
Checkpoints SHA-256 verified

The store outlives every window
The asset server is its own daemon, so closing one app never drops the catalog for the others.
Asset UI, VJ and workers are clients
Restart detected in about 3.5 s
Clients rejoin automatically
One server per root, enforced

Takeaway
Makepad treats UI, physics, and generative AI as one Rust stack, with no external crates for the physics and no Python for the AI.

posts.alt: Observatory: Curiosity, Experiment, Trace
posts.caption: Pose a question. Run it in real physics. Keep the trace. Observatory is a browser workbench that turns a "what if" into a running experiment. It began as a real-ephemeris solar system and grew into ten instruments on one shared engine. The newest one trains a tiny fly to find scent, with honest limits stated up front.
posts.body:
Pose a question. Run it in real physics. Keep the trace.
Observatory: a lab notebook and a telescope in one browser window.

Curiosity, experiment, trace
Ask a question, drive a live model with real controls, then keep the evidence.
What if the Sun lost half its mass?
Perturb the system while it runs
Trails, timeline, version commits, PNG snapshots

One engine, many instruments
10
Solar System, Equation, Earth, Light, Gravity, Photo, Diffusion, Fractals, Tesseract and Fly Expedition share one renderer, camera, trails and HUD.

Scent Seekers: train a fly
Create a specimen, run 200 learning episodes, then launch an orchard expedition against untrained and reactive controls under matched seeds.
Tile-coded SARSA(lambda) in a Web Worker
95% Wilson intervals on success counts
Saved locally in IndexedDB, no server

What the audit found
84.7% vs 2%
Varied training averaged 84.7% success against 2% untrained on 50 held-out worlds. One seed scored only 27 of 50, so variability is material.

Honest about its limits
A reduced software model, not whole-brain emulation. It uses an engineered steering prior and privileged reward shaping during training.

Takeaway: keep the trace
A good experiment leaves evidence you can return to, compare, and share.
Report Scout ranks files and cites sources
100% coverage, on synthetic data only
Exports portable JSON, runs offline

posts.alt: Flow Lab: Play With Navier-Stokes
posts.caption: Stir a fluid in your browser and watch the physics happen Flow Lab is an interactive fluid mechanics lab that runs fully offline in one HTML file. Stir, draw obstacles, and switch between dye, velocity, pressure and vorticity to see what each term of the Navier-Stokes equations actually does. It is a qualitative learning tool, not a validated engineering solver.
posts.body:
Stir a fluid in your browser and watch the physics happen
Flow Lab: an interactive Navier-Stokes playground.

What it is
An educational fluid mechanics lab with adjustable parameters, four experiments, and synchronized measurements. One HTML file, no server, no internet needed.

What you can do
Stir, inject dye, draw or erase obstacles
Place a probe and read its history
Tune viscosity and inlet speed
Switch dye, velocity, pressure, vorticity views
Rotate a height-field view of the data

Four guided experiments
See what pressure does
Make a vortex disappear
Squeeze the stream
Follow the momentum

Key insight
Each equation term gets its own lesson. Turn off advection, diffusion or pressure correction and see the flow break. Raising viscosity makes vortex kinetic energy decay faster.

How it works
2D incompressible fluid on a staggered MAC grid. Semi-Lagrangian momentum transport, explicit viscous diffusion with an adaptive timestep, and iterative pressure projection.

Honest about limits
A qualitative learning model, not validated engineering CFD and not 3D turbulence. The surface view is a height plot of 2D data, not a real free surface.

posts.alt: Cloning an AI outbound-sales platform
posts.caption: We cloned an AI sales platform to study its UX, then gave it a real backend A local clone of Autospawn, an AI outbound-sales platform, built to study the product's UX. It started as mock data and grew a real Next.js backend powered by the Claude Agent SDK. The twist: every agent call has a fallback, so it works with zero auth.
posts.body:
We cloned an AI sales platform to study its UX
Agents that find customers the moment they want to buy.

Features cloned
10
Dispatch composer, campaigns, lead dossier, watcher, inbox, analytics, sequences, profile, credits, integrations.

How a run works
You describe who to target. The agent reads the ICP, scans sources, qualifies, enriches, then lands you in a new campaign with leads.

A real backend, same app
Every flow goes through Next.js route handlers.
JSON store with atomic writes
Credit ledger for every debit
Claude Agent SDK runs the agent
Composio powers live Connections
Empty balance returns HTTP 402

Never breaks without auth
No API key? It uses your own Claude Code login. No login at all? A deterministic fallback generator runs, and responses say via: claude or fallback.

Credits enforced server-side
24 / 8
Dispatch costs 24 credits. Getting more leads costs 8.

Takeaway
Leads are fictional by design and the brand is borrowed. Great for studying UX, rebrand before going public.

posts.alt: linear-clone: a Linear-style view of XO data
posts.caption: We cloned Linear's UI, with no database behind it linear-clone is a Linear-style tracker with issues, OKRs, sprints, a calendar and a wiki. Its backend is just the .xo files that XO agents leave on disk. The app reads them and never writes back. That keeps the data honest and the UI swappable.
posts.body:
We cloned Linear's UI, with no database behind it
Issues, OKRs, sprints and a wiki, powered by files on disk.

What it is
A Linear-style tracker with a dark, dense, keyboard-driven UI. It is a visualizer for XO data plus a simple work-item tool.
Issues, OKRs, sprints
Calendar, members, wiki
C for new issue, Cmd K for palette

The backend is the .xo files
Agents leave todos.json and work-items.json on disk. The app mirrors them as issues, members and projects. It never writes to them.

Setup is one variable
3 steps
XO root resolves from the Setup dialog, then the XO_ROOT env var, then the topmost ancestor folder containing .xo.

Two kinds of state
Mirror data resyncs on every load. Local data sticks around.
Mirror: issues, members, projects
Local: sprints, OKRs, wiki
Local lives in localStorage
Edits to mirrored data vanish on sync

Store actions are the contract
Every mutation is a named zustand action. Write back later means swapping action bodies for API calls. No feature UI changes.

Takeaway
Treat agent files as the source of truth, mirror them read only, and keep the UI behind a clean action contract.

posts.alt: Does Project Context Help Coding Agents?
posts.caption: We gave a coding agent 6 levels of context. Here's what changed. A pilot study on Structured Agent Environments: does richer project context (nothing, README, AGENTS.md, full XO scaffold, scaffold plus seeded memory) help a coding agent orient faster and spend fewer tokens? Early Codex results on one task show the trend: more context, fewer effective tokens. The harness is now hermetic and multi-operator, so collaborators can run slices and merge results.
posts.body:
Does context make coding agents cheaper?
Six environments. Ten tasks. One question: does project structure change how an agent works?

The research question
Does richer project context let a coding agent orient faster and spend fewer tokens, without hurting task success?

Six environments, one codebase
Same source snapshot, only the overlay files change.
E0: nothing
E1: README
E2: AGENTS.md
E3: AGENTS.md + PROJECT.md
E4 and E5: full XO scaffold, E5 adds seeded memory

How a run works
Each cell is one agent run of one task (T01 to T10) in one environment. Every run gets its own git worktree cut from a pinned SHA, and telemetry is extracted from the transcript afterward.

Early signal: T01 effective tokens
317k > 278k > 216k
E0, E1, E2 on Codex. About 96% of input was cached, so the cache-discounted total is the meaningful cost metric.

Bugs found along the way
Running a pilot exposes the harness flaws.
A run leaked code into an unrelated checkout
T02 passed with no changes (false 1.0)
4 task YAMLs failed to parse
E5 memory files were empty, so E5 had less than E4

Takeaway
The harness is now hermetic and tagged per operator, so collaborators can run slices and merge results. Early trend: more context, fewer tokens. Full study pending.

posts.alt: Sandbox Space Smoke Test
posts.caption: The safest experiment is one that holds nothing at all A tiny generated fixture used to check that one-click sandbox launch works end to end. It checks the sandbox-local Space URL and follow-up Agents API turns. It holds no user data, so it is safe to poke at.
posts.body:
The safest experiment is one that holds nothing at all
Meet the Sandbox Space smoke test.

What it is
Generated content used to verify that a one-click sandbox launch works.

What it verifies
One-click sandbox launch
The sandbox-local Space URL
Follow-up Agents API turns

Built to be harmless
The fixture is generated and intentionally non-sensitive. It contains no user data.

A fenced-in agent
During verification, the sandbox agent may inspect and modify only the copied workspace.

Takeaway
Test launches with fake, non-sensitive data in a copied workspace, so a failure costs nothing.

posts.alt: Git history as a flowing wave
posts.caption: What if a git branch looked like a breathing green and red wave? XO Visualizer turns any local repo's history into a calm, histography-style wave. Additions rise as a green ridge, deletions fall as red. It is plain Canvas 2D, built on Next.js 16 and React 19, and all git access stays server-side.
posts.body:
What if a git branch looked like a breathing wave?
XO Visualizer: a histography-style view of repo history.

One branch, one wave
Each commit adds a soft Gaussian bump. Summed across the width, they become a flowing ridge, not a spiky bar chart.

How to read it
Green ridge up: additions
Red ridge down: deletions
Horizontal: commit order
Height compressed with value^0.6
Hover to snap to a commit

It feels alive
A slow traveling ripple modulates amplitude, with a soft white sweep. On branch switch or Replay, the wave streams in left to right with ease-out.

Git stays on the server
A Route Handler runs git log --numstat via execFile, with no shell, so paths cannot inject commands. The browser never touches the filesystem.

Beyond the wave (v0.2.0)
Run the working tree in a split pane
Dev-server process manager
Experiment button: worktree plus Claude session
Live working-state card

Takeaway
Restraint and gentle motion make data feel alive. No heavy deps, just Canvas 2D and a calm idea.

posts.alt: TimesFM: GPT for Time Series
posts.caption: Forecast any time series without training a model. Google's TimesFM does it. TimesFM is Google Research's pretrained decoder-only model for zero-shot forecasting. Feed it a history of numbers and it predicts what comes next, with confidence bands, and no per-series training. Version 2.5 is smaller and handles far longer context, and it already ships in BigQuery, Sheets and Vertex.
posts.body:
Forecast anything. Train nothing.
TimesFM: Google's foundation model for time series. Think GPT, but for numbers over time.

What it is
A pretrained decoder-only model (ICML 2024). Give it a history, get the next stretch back, often with confidence bands. Zero-shot, no training on your data.

Why it matters
Classical and deep models usually need per-series training, tuning and upkeep. TimesFM aims for decent forecasts out of the box, so teams focus on decisions.

Pretraining scale
100B+
Real-world time-points, including Google Trends and Wikipedia pageviews. It learned trend, seasonality and spikes, then applies them to unseen series.

TimesFM 2.5 vs 2.0
A smaller model with much longer memory.
200M parameters, down from 500M
16k context, up from 2048
Quantile forecasts up to 1k horizon
No frequency indicator needed
Covariates via XReg

Where it gets used
Anywhere there is a timestamp and a metric.
Retail demand and inventory
Payments volume and liquidity
Bike-share and ops capacity
Anomaly detection from forecast bands
BigQuery, Sheets, Vertex

The takeaway
Forecasting as a foundation capability, not a custom science project every time. Use tuned models when you need explainability or heavy covariates.

posts.alt: Tiny World Builder
posts.caption: A whole 3D voxel world editor, in one browser tab Tiny World Builder is a self-contained 3D voxel world editor that runs in the browser. You can place terrain, sculpt cliffs and rivers, fly around, and share your worlds. It even has road-following AI cars that reroute around anything you drop on the street.
posts.body:
Build tiny 3D worlds right in your browser
Tiny World Builder: build, sculpt, fly, share.

Four things you can do
Build: terrain, props, homes, paths, crops, animals
Fly: switch camera modes, explore every angle
Sculpt: raise, lower, paint into cliffs and rivers
Share: save, remix, export, open to real players

Smart tiles that adapt
Place a neighbor and surrounding cells re-render. Roads join, rivers get banks, fences connect, and houses form L, T, + or square buildings.

Lines of vanilla JS
~29k
One script block, organised by section comments. The world is split into intent cells and a renderer.

Cars that react to your edits
Vehicles drive only on path cells. Drop a rock or tree on a road and active cars reroute, or stop if no alternate path exists.

Hackable by design
Outbound webhooks for cell events
Inbound SSE commands
A minimal MCP bridge over stdio
Seeded demo URLs to share traffic scenes

Takeaway
A full world editor with tools, AI traffic, and plugin hooks, shipped as a static site with Three.js self-hosted.

posts.alt: Galaxy sandbox: your Claude sessions as galaxies
posts.caption: Every Claude Code session on my machine is now a galaxy Galaxy sandbox is an interactive particle simulation where thousands of stars orbit galaxy cores under softened gravity. Its Sessions scene turns every Claude Code session on your machine into its own galaxy, sized by message count and colored by project. Click one, prompt it, and watch it come alive.
posts.body:
Every Claude Code session on my machine is now a galaxy
Galaxy sandbox: stars, gravity, and your chat history.

What it is
Thousands of stars orbit galaxy cores under softened gravity. Close passes pull spiral arms into tidal tails, and slow encounters merge cores.

The Sessions scene
It opens here by default. Each session becomes a galaxy.
Sized by message count
Colored by project
Your current session glows lime at the center
Click a galaxy to see title, size, last active

Active sessions move
90 sec
Any session written to in the last 90 seconds gets a pulsing core, faster orbit, and a green activity dot.

Prompt a galaxy
Type in the card and it runs claude --resume <id> -p in that session's folder. Same transcript, same history. Live sessions are skipped to avoid clashing writes.

How it stays cheap
Dozens of galaxies run smoothly.
Session cores ride prescribed golden-angle orbits
Each star only feels its own core
Typed arrays per galaxy
Canvas 2D with additive blending
Trails come from fading, not clearing

Takeaway
Your work history becomes something you can see and poke. The server reads files and spawns the CLI, so the browser never touches your filesystem.

posts.alt: Marble Skill Taxonomy: a map of learning
posts.caption: 1,590 things kids learn, wired into one prerequisite graph Marble released an open taxonomy of what children learn in the primary years. It breaks learning into 1,590 micro-topics and links them with 3,221 prerequisite edges, each with a one-line reason. It is aligned to national standards like Common Core and the UK National Curriculum, and free to use in products under ODbL.
posts.body:
1,590 things kids learn, wired into one graph
Marble Skill Taxonomy v1: an open map of primary school learning.

Prerequisite links
3,221
Each edge says topic X depends on prerequisite Y, tagged hard or soft, with a one-line reason.

Not a flat list of standards
Each micro-topic is one teachable idea, like 'Building sentences', with a plain description, mastery evidence, a type and an age range.

Eight subjects
Science: 547
Mathematics: 503
English: 286
History: 90
Personal & Social Development: 88

Reasons, not just links
Example: 'Must understand vibrations make sound before finding volume patterns'. The graph explains why order matters.

Aligned to real standards
Topics link to NGSS, Common Core and the UK National Curriculum. 183 parent-friendly cluster summaries are included too.

Take it and build
Pure JSON, no runtime. Commercial use is allowed with attribution. Only improvements to the taxonomy itself must stay open.

posts.alt: One idea, five forms, one rail
posts.caption: What if one idea could evolve from terminal to live app, and you could scrub the whole history? Artifact Evolution is a prototype where a single idea moves through five forms: terminal, markdown one-pager, deck, notebook, and Next.js app. Every form is saved as an immutable artifact, so you can scrub back through the whole history in the browser. The demo run turns a churn analysis into a shipped dashboard.
posts.body:
One idea. Five forms. One rail.
A prototype where work evolves from terminal to app, and every step is kept.

The five forms
Each promotion rewrites the same idea in a new shape.
Terminal session
Markdown one-pager
Reveal-style deck
Jupyter notebook
Next.js app

The demo run
14.2%
Monthly churn, up from 11.4%. 71% of the rise is starter accounts cancelling in 30 days. It became a dashboard in 5 steps.

Append-only history
Artifacts are immutable. Rolling back HEAD just re-points it, so the future is never deleted and you can fast-forward again.

Three ways to view it
A toggle in the header switches modes.
Work: stage, metadata, rail, promote bar
Diff: parent vs child, with carried, added, dropped
Movie: full-screen autoplay every 4.5s

Watch Claude write it
Click Evolve and the next form streams in token by token over SSE. A new node then pops onto the rail.

Honest about what is fake
The promoter is mocked, pub/sub is in-process, and there is no auth. One Promoter interface is the seam to swap in a real Claude-backed version.

posts.alt: How a Tree Eats Air
posts.caption: 95% of a tree's mass came from thin air, not soil An interactive carbon and oxygen simulation that follows a tree from seed to giant, from one leaf's chemistry up to centuries of growth. Nearly half a tree's dry weight is carbon that was floating in the air as CO₂. Watch it get built, one 29 minute step at a time.
posts.body:
95% of a tree's mass came from thin air, not soil
A simulation of how a tree turns CO₂ into wood.

The reaction behind it all
6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂. Exactly 1 O₂ is released for every CO₂ fixed.

Three scales, one sim
The model links the leaf to the whole tree to centuries of growth.
Leaf: light reactions and the Calvin cycle
Tree: carbon becomes leaves, stem, branches, roots
Time: growth from seed through +1000 years

Counter-intuitive part
Dry biomass is about 50% carbon. Roots mostly drink water and borrow a few minerals. The wood is built from air.

Respiration eats a lot
~50%
Autotrophic respiration burns roughly half of gross photosynthesis. The rest, NPP, becomes biomass. At night the tree emits CO₂.

Van Helmont's willow
In 5 years it gained about 74 kg while the soil lost only about 57 g. He credited water, but he had proven the mass isn't from soil.

Take it away
A tree is mostly captured air. You can step through every equation, or run 1000 years, and watch it happen.

posts.alt: Grow a Fractal Tree From Git History
posts.caption: Every commit hash grows its own branch of a fractal tree Fractal Lab is an interactive canvas playground for fractals, with a Commit Journey mode that turns a repo's real git history into a tree. Each commit hash decides how one generation of branches grows, so the same commit always grows the same way. Your project's story becomes a shape you can watch unfold.
posts.body:
Your git history, grown as a fractal tree
Each commit hash seeds one generation. The journey is the growth.

Fractal Lab
An interactive canvas playground built with Next.js. It renders Mandelbrot, Julia, Burning Ship, Sierpinski, Barnsley Fern and a Fractal Tree.

Real data in
A server route runs git log on any repo path. It reads hash, author, date, subject, additions, deletions and files changed for up to 1000 commits.

A hash becomes a branch
Pairs of hex characters from the hash set the traits of one generation.
Branch angle: 14 to 48 degrees
Left child length: 0.60 to 0.78
Right child length: 0.58 to 0.76
Lean and twist for asymmetry
A base hue fingerprint

Same commit, same shape
0 randomness
Every trait is a pure function of the hash, so a given commit always grows the same way.

Play with the growth
Reveal commits one by one and watch the silhouette morph.
Color by journey, author or palette
Animated growth timer
Optional leaves and sway
Offline sample data as fallback

Takeaway
Deterministic hashes turn ordinary commit logs into unique, repeatable art.

posts.alt: Agent Sandboxes on Nirvana
posts.caption: Spin up an isolated agent sandbox in about 2.5 seconds Nirvana Agent Sandboxes give autonomous agents isolated, managed environments on NKS infrastructure. You create, pause, resume and delete them through a simple API. Persistent mode keeps files across pauses, so long-running agents can pick up where they left off.
posts.body:
A sandbox for your agent in 2.5 seconds
Isolated, managed environments for autonomous agents on Nirvana's NKS infra.

Ephemeral create time
~2.5s
Persistent sandboxes with storage take about 6 to 7 seconds.

Full lifecycle, one API
Create: POST /sandboxes
Pause and resume, instantly
Delete: permanent, no recovery
Logs, events and inspect for debugging
List and get status any time

Pause frees compute, keeps files
On pause the pod is deleted but the PVC is retained. On resume a new pod re-mounts the same storage at /workspace.

Two ways to reach a service
Gateway: fast data plane, best for real traffic
Header: OpenSandbox-Ingress-To: {id}-{port}
Proxy: simple, routes via the API server
Proxy has lower throughput

Ephemeral or persistent
Ephemeral is memory-only and starts fastest. Persistent mounts a PVC, from 50Gi local-path for dev to ABS block storage for prod.

Checkpoint, don't restart
Agents write state to /workspace and resume from the last recorded step instead of starting over.

posts.alt: Galaxy Sandbox: Hurl Your Own Galaxy
posts.caption: Throw a galaxy at another galaxy and watch what happens Galaxy sandbox is an interactive space simulation. Drag on the canvas to hurl a new galaxy and see how it interacts with the others. Close passes tear spiral arms into tidal tails, while slow encounters merge cores.
posts.body:
Throw a galaxy at another galaxy
Galaxy sandbox: an interactive collision simulator.

How you play
Drag on space to hurl a new galaxy. Or press Add galaxy and watch it join the scene.

Close passes
Tidal tails
When galaxies swing close, spiral arms are torn into long tidal tails.

Slow encounters
Merger
When galaxies meet slowly, their cores merge.

Controls to play with
Pause and Reset
Add galaxy
Speed (1.0x default)
Gravity (1.0x default)
Trails on or off

Takeaway
Change the speed or gravity and see how the same encounter ends differently.

posts.alt: Paperclip: The Company for Your AI Agents
posts.caption: If OpenClaw is an employee, Paperclip is the company Paperclip is an open-source Node.js server and React UI that orchestrates a team of AI agents to run a business. It looks like a task manager, but adds org charts, budgets, governance and goal alignment. Manage business goals, not pull requests.
posts.body:
If OpenClaw is an employee, Paperclip is the company
Open-source orchestration for zero-human companies.

What it is
A Node.js server and React UI that orchestrates a team of AI agents. Bring your own agents, assign goals, track work and costs from one dashboard.

Three steps to run
Manage business goals, not pull requests.
Define the goal, like a $1M MRR app
Hire the team: CEO, CTO, engineers, marketers
Approve strategy, set budgets, hit go

Bring your own agent
Any agent, any runtime, one org chart. If it can receive a heartbeat, it's hired. Works with OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Bash and HTTP.

Built like a real company
It looks like a task manager, but under the hood:
Org charts with roles and reporting lines
Heartbeats: agents wake on a schedule and act
Goal alignment: every task traces to the mission
Monthly budgets per agent, they stop at the limit
Immutable audit log with tool-call tracing

You are the board
Approve hires, override strategy, pause or terminate any agent at any time. One deployment can host many isolated companies.

Takeaway
Stop juggling 20 Claude Code terminals. Give your agents an org chart, a budget and a boss: you.

posts.alt: Code That Renders Video
posts.caption: We made videos with React components, not a video editor my-video is a Remotion project where video is just React code. It animates code snippets with Code Hike and also holds two branded XO videos, a Clawdbot intro and an Autonomous Digital Agency pitch. Every frame is a function of the frame number, so videos can be versioned, diffed and re-rendered like software.
posts.body:
Video, written as React code
A Remotion project that renders animated code walkthroughs and XO promo videos.

Code snippets become scenes
Drop files named code1.tsx, code2.tsx in public. Each file is one step, and tokens glide between steps using Code Hike transitions.

How the pipeline works
Read code* files from public
Run TypeScript through twoslash for types and errors
Highlight with one of 22 themes
Measure the widest line to size the video
Render each step for 90 frames

Duration is computed
90 frames
Each snippet gets 90 frames, so length is file count times 90. Width is rounded to even because MP4 requires it.

Live reload while editing
The studio watches the public folder. Change a code file and the composition re-evaluates automatically.

Two XO videos live here too
ClawdbotVideo: 450 frames, 1920x1080
XOAgencyVideo: 1800 frames, 1920x1080
Both at 30 fps, built from springs and interpolations
Hook: What if your agency never slept?

Takeaway
When video is code, you can version it, diff it, and re-render it on demand.

posts.alt: Remotion Studio: Video in React
posts.caption: What if you could render an MP4 from a React component? Remotion Studio is a small starter project for making video with React code. Pin the versions, run one command to preview, run another to render an MP4. It is a clean way to see video as code instead of a timeline.
posts.body:
Render an MP4 from a React component
A tiny Remotion starter project.

What it is
remotion-studio v1.0.0 is a simple Remotion starter project. Video is built from React, not a timeline editor.

The stack
remotion 4.0.242
@remotion/cli 4.0.242
React 18.3
TypeScript 5.7
Only 4 runtime dependencies

Two commands run it
Preview, then render.
start: npx remotion studio
build: npx remotion render
Entry: src/index.ts
Composition: HelloWorld
Output: out/video.mp4

Why it is interesting
Core and CLI are pinned to the same exact version, so renders stay predictable. An upgrade script keeps them in sync.

Video is just code
Write a component, preview it live, render it to MP4. Same workflow as any React app.
